With a low groan of disuse, a section of the library's shelving swung inward, presenting the Stygian maw of a forgotten servant's passage. Revolver in his right hand, the lantern held low in his left, Julian risked a quick look into the gloom. He returned a moment later, his expression one of grim satisfaction. "As I thought," he breathed; "Caldwell’s men are watching the street and the garden gate. They have no knowledge of the house’s intestines. Now, quickly...." Moving to the grand fireplace, he seized a heavy iron poker. With three sharp blows, he shattered the face of the ornate mantelpiece clock, its delicate hands frozen forever at a quarter past two. "A bit of misdirection!" he explained, a wry smile touching his lips. "They will hear the crash; they will assume we are smashing furniture, searching for a last desperate weapon. It will make them cautious, and caution will make them slow.... Every second we can purchase is worth a king's ransom.... Now, another thing." The lantern’s beam found her face. He took her hand, which lay cold and still in his. "I have led you into this morass, Eleonora, with my cursed arrogance," he said, his voice low and urgent; "I believed my past was buried deep enough. Now we must prepare for the worst, for the possibility of being separated in the city's web.... Varga will have men at the train stations and the docks; he is as thorough as he is cruel. We cannot return to our hotel, and we have not the funds for another. There is only one place I can think of, a place of public anonymity.... The Giardini Pubblici, at the easternmost tip of the city." Her fingers tightened, a faint tremor running through them. "I understand," she replied, her voice barely a whisper; "if we are parted, I am to make my way to the Public Gardens and wait for you by the main gate." "Precisely! ...Though God grant we have no need of it." Like conspirators in some forbidden play, they plunged into the narrow passage, through a musty cellar redolent of damp earth and soured wine, and emerged into a tiny, walled courtyard overgrown with ivy. From there, a low iron gate, its lock long since rusted away, gave them egress into a silent, narrow alleyway. The fog, rolling in from the lagoon, coiled about their ankles and muffled their footsteps. To the few late-night stragglers they passed, they must have appeared as nothing more than a pair of lovers stealing a last moment before parting, Julian with the collar of his worn coat turned up against the damp, Eleonora a slender shadow at his side.... He led her not toward the great canals but through a warren of back streets to a small, secluded traghetto stop, where for a few near-worthless coins a grizzled old man ferried them across the water in his sandolo. They disembarked in a district of artisans and laborers, and within minutes were seated in the secluded corner of a smoky osteria, the air thick with the scent of fried fish and cheap red wine. They ate ravenously: the food was simple, the wine sharp, but it was hot and nourishing, a balm to their frayed nerves. Julian felt a great weight lift from his shoulders. Their escape, for the moment, was complete. His confidence, a thing he had always possessed in prodigious measure, returned to him tenfold. He was young, he was audacious, he was free. And the peril they shared wove a thread of profound intimacy through their silence. For the first time, Julian found himself wanting to shed the layers of cynicism and deceit that had been his armour for so long. And encouraged by her quiet, unwavering attention, he began to speak of himself; of his early days as a penniless scholar, his fall from grace; of the insidious craft of the forger, the intellectual thrill of creating a lie so perfect it could alter the past; of the man named Varga, whose collection was built on such lies; of his decision, made in the moment he first saw her, to live an authentic life, whatever the cost. And Eleonora, her chin resting in her palm, listened with the profound seriousness that women often grant the confessions of men they are beginning to love. Of her own history, she revealed almost nothing: Julian filled in the blanks himself, painting a portrait of a companion, a gentlewoman of reduced circumstances, caught in Varga's gilded web. Yet sometimes her clear grey eyes would grow troubled, her attention seeming to drift, as if some phrase of his had unlocked a private and painful memory. "I am wearying you with my history," he said once, struck by a sudden pang of guilt at his own monologue. She started, as if returning from a great distance. "No, not at all.... But I must wonder, do you truly grasp what you are leaving behind?" "A life of lies," he stated with conviction; "it is not a great loss. The challenge now is to build something true." "But," she pressed gently, "you told me your talent was the one thing that gave you pride, a sense of power over a world that had rejected you. You believe a resolution made in a moment of crisis can truly supplant the habits and comforts of your entire existence? I believe in your sincerity now, tonight; but what of the morning, and all the mornings after, when you are poor and unknown, and remember the respect, the fear, your old skills commanded?" "If I am tempted, then I will remember what I stand to gain.... It seems to me that the desire for truth is proof that one is not entirely false." "I want to believe that, and yet..." She looked down at her hands, twisting a small, plain ring on her finger. "You say this change is for me, that I am the cause of this sudden quest for honesty. What... what if you were to learn that I am not what you think I am?" "Impossible," he said, his voice firm. A faint, sorrowful smile touched her lips, a look of deep and weary knowledge. "But what if it were true--?" "Then," he said, his voice dropping, "I think there would be nothing left to build on." "And you would return to your old life--?" "How can I say?" he asked, his bravado gone. "It is not a question I can answer. I only know that it would take a monumental deception to destroy my belief in you!" "You feel that way now," she murmured. "But if I had lied to you--?" "Eleonora!" He reached across the rough-hewn table, his hand covering hers. "There is no point in these suppositions. You must know--" She pulled her hand away as if his touch had burned her, a sharp intake of breath her only reply. "No!" "But I must tell you. I have spent my life in the company of shadows, and you are the first light I have known.... I love you; it is the hope of being worthy of you that has given me the strength to turn my back on my past. Perhaps you are promised to another; that is a risk I will take. Perhaps there is some secret sorrow you carry that makes you doubt my resolve. That, only time can answer. But you must understand this: if I should fail, the fault will be mine alone; it will be a flaw in my own character, not in your inspiration.... All I ask is what you have already given me: this chance, this night.... And at the end of it, when we are safe, if you tell me to go, I will go, and I will not blame you; for a man cannot build a true life upon a foundation he has stolen--"

She did not respond at once; she seemed incapable of it. The hand she had snatched away now rested upon the crumpled tablecloth, her fingers tracing the crease of a fold as if it were a line in a book of fates she could not decipher. Her gaze, when at last she raised it to his, was clouded with a sorrow so profound it eclipsed the candlelight.

"And what if," she began, her voice a near-whisper, "what if the very ground upon which you hope to build is not yours to claim? What if the inspiration, as you call it, is itself... a kind of theft?"

"I don't understand you," he said, and the bewilderment in his tone was genuine. The triumphant certainty that had buoyed him all evening was beginning to founder on the rocks of her strange, persistent melancholy. "Eleonora... what are you trying to tell me?"

"Perhaps only that you see me as a symbol," she continued, her eyes straying from his to some point in the middle distance, "a statue of virtue you have erected in your own mind. You are in love not with me, but with your own noble resolution; and I am merely the pedestal for it. And pedestals, Marcel... they are often made of very common stone."

The use of his old name, the name of the drudge, the shadow-dweller, struck him like a physical blow. He recoiled slightly, a frown knitting his brows. "That is not true. And it is not fair. I see you, the woman before me. The rest is... sophistry. You are trying to drive me away."

"Am I?" A wan smile touched her lips, a fleeting ghost of an expression. "Or am I trying to save you from a future disappointment so bitter it would poison the very memory of this night?"

Before he could formulate a reply, a rap on the door heralded the return of their waiter, a stout, cheerful man with a napkin draped over his arm. He entered bearing the bill on a small pewter plate, which he set down with a discreet cough and a murmured, "Whenever you are ready, Monsieur."

The intrusion, mundane as it was, shattered the tense intimacy of their exchange. It brought Lanyard crashing back to earth; to the reality of their situation, of the empty pocketbook and the watching city. He drew out his "emaciated purse" and counted out the notes, adding a tip that was, by his old standards, pitiably small, but which represented a significant portion of his remaining capital. The waiter, oblivious, beamed his thanks and departed.

There remained, as Lanyard had calculated, barely enough for a cab fare to some distant, hypothetical safety. The knowledge, which an hour ago had been a point of pride, a proof of his devil-may-care reliance on his own wits, now felt like a leaden weight in his stomach. His grand resolution seemed suddenly a flimsy, foolish thing in the face of her doubt and their shared penury.

"We should go," he said, his voice flat.

He helped her with her coat, his fingers brushing her shoulders. It was a gesture he had performed with a light heart only hours earlier; now it felt freighted with an unnameable significance, as if he were clothing a stranger. They descended the narrow, creaking stairs and passed through the now-empty dining room, its proprietor bidding them a sleepy "Bonne nuit."

Then they were outside, plunged once more into the damp embrace of the Parisian night. The mist had thickened into a fine, persistent drizzle that clung to their clothes and beaded in her hair. The lively clatter of Les Halles was a muted rumble in the distance; here, in the labyrinth of narrow streets, a profound silence reigned, broken only by the drip of water from a gargoyle's stone mouth and the soft echo of their own footsteps on the glistening cobblestones.

They walked without speaking, the chasm of their recent conversation yawning between them. Lanyard, his mind a turmoil of hurt pride and a dawning, terrible anxiety, steered them eastward through a warren of black alleys and sleeping courtyards he knew from another life; a life he had, only this evening, so confidently declared finished. The irony was not lost on him. He was using the knowledge of the Lone Wolf to guide the reformed man, a paradox that mirrored the very one she had thrown in his face.

"Where are we going?" she asked at last, her voice small in the vast quiet.

"Away from the main boulevards," he answered, not looking at her. "We cannot afford another cab, and the subways will be closing soon. We must walk. I thought... toward the river. We can follow it for a time; there is always cover there."

He felt the light pressure of her hand on his arm. "Marcel... I did not mean to..."

"Don't," he cut in, more harshly than he intended. He softened his tone. "Please. Let us not speak of it now. We are still not safe. Popinot's resources are not inconsiderable; it would be like him to have men watching the restaurants, even the small ones."

As if his words had conjured the threat, he saw it: a flicker of movement in the deep shadow of a porte-cochère fifty yards ahead. It was nothing, perhaps; a cat, a scrap of paper caught in the wind. But Lanyard's senses, honed by years of living on the knife-edge of peril, screamed a silent alarm. He halted so abruptly that she stumbled against him.

"What is it?" she whispered, her fear a palpable thing.

He did not answer immediately. His eyes, preternaturally sharp in the gloom, strained to dissect the shadows. He saw the man now, a silhouette, indistinct but for the tell-tale posture of one who waits. The man lit a cigarette, the brief flare of the match illuminating a narrow, rat-like face Lanyard knew all too well: a petty apache named Le Corbeau, a man who would sell his own mother for the price of a drink and who, Lanyard knew for a fact, had lately fallen into Popinot's orbit.

"A friend of our host," Lanyard murmured, his voice grim. He pushed her gently but firmly backward, into the deeper darkness of a recessed doorway. "Stay here. Do not move, and do not make a sound, no matter what happens."

His mind raced, sifting through possibilities with the cold, swift precision of a calculating machine. To fight was folly; Le Corbeau would not be alone. To run was to invite a chase they could not win on foot. There remained only guile; the old, familiar weapon he had sworn to lay down. Her words echoed in his head: *you've only to take one step aside to gain a smooth and easy way.* Was this it, then? The first test?

He glanced at her, a pale shape huddled in the doorway, her eyes wide and dark with terror. And in that moment, all the intellectual debate, all the philosophical wrangling of the past hour, evaporated. The question was no longer abstract. Her safety was the only axiom, the one fixed point in his reeling universe.

"I will be back," he whispered, and turning, he melted into the shadows, moving with a silent, fluid grace that was the antithesis of the honest, straightforward man he had resolved to become.

He did not go far. He circled the block, using an alley he remembered that ran behind the buildings. It was foul-smelling and slick with refuse, but it brought him out on a parallel street. From there, it was a simple matter to approach the porte-cochère from the opposite direction. He flattened himself against a wall, his heart pounding a slow, steady rhythm, his entire being focused on the task at hand. He was the Lone Wolf again, and he felt the grim, intoxicating thrill of the hunt.

He waited. Minutes stretched into an eternity. At last, he heard what he had been listening for: a low whistle from down the street, a signal. Le Corbeau straightened, flicked his cigarette into the gutter, and began to walk away from his post, heading toward the source of the sound. Lanyard gave him a twenty-second lead, then followed.

He shadowed the man for two blocks, to the corner of the rue de Rivoli. Here, another figure detached itself from the gloom of the arcades. The two men met, spoke in low tones. Lanyard was too far away to hear the words, but the gestures were plain enough: a shrug from Le Corbeau, an impatient chop of the hand from the newcomer. A report was being made; a failure was being admitted. Popinot's net had, for the moment, come up empty.

Lanyard watched them separate, Le Corbeau shuffling off into the night, the other man striding purposefully toward the Tuileries. Only then did he allow himself to breathe. He had gambled on Popinot's patience, and won. The search in this sector was being called off, at least for now.

He made his way back to the doorway where he had left her. The journey, which had taken him nearly fifteen minutes, seemed to have lasted a lifetime. He found her just as he had left her, a statue of terrified obedience pressed into the stone recess.

"It's all right," he said softly, his voice emerging as a croak. He cleared his throat. "They've gone. We are safe, for a little while."

She did not fly into his arms with relief. She simply sagged against the wall, a puppet whose strings had been cut. He reached out and took her arm, and this time she did not resist. Her flesh was cold as ice, even through the fabric of her coat.

"You were gone so long," she said, her voice trembling. "I thought..."

"I had to be certain," he said. "They were calling in the watchdogs. We have a few hours, perhaps, before they cast the net again. We must use them."

He led her out of the doorway and into the street. The drizzle had stopped, and a sliver of moon now shone through a ragged tear in the clouds, bathing the wet rooftops in a ghostly silver light. They walked on, their footsteps a lonely counterpoint to the city's sleeping heartbeat. The brief, sharp thrill of the chase had faded, leaving Lanyard with a sour taste in his mouth. He had not failed the test, perhaps; but he had not passed it in the way he had hoped. He had used the wolf's cunning to save the man, and he did not know whether to feel pride or shame.

They reached the Pont Neuf and paused, leaning against the cold stone parapet. Below them, the Seine flowed black and silent, its surface littered with shimmering reflections. In the distance, the skeletal form of the Eiffel Tower was a charcoal sketch against the clearing sky. Paris lay spread before them, a city of infinite beauty and infinite menace.

"Marcel," she said, her voice now steady, imbued with a strange, quiet resolution. "There is something I must tell you. Something you should have known from the beginning."

He turned to face her. Her profile was outlined against the moonlit water, as delicate and as remote as a cameo. "I am listening," he said.

"My name," she began, and her hesitation was so slight he almost missed it, "is not Eleonora Shannon."

Lanyard said nothing. He felt a peculiar stillness descend upon him, a profound and terrible calm. It was as if he had been anticipating this blow without knowing it; as if his body had been braced for it all along.

"My family is not... good. It is not even my family. The story I told you, of a young woman obliged to become self-supporting... it is a lie. Every word of it." She took a breath, a ragged, painful sound. "My real name is Lucia. And my father... my father is a man you know. Or a man you knew of, in your former life. His name is Count Victor Dubroc."

Lanyard felt the world tilt on its axis. Dubroc. The name echoed down the dark corridors of his memory. Victor Dubroc, the "Count of Counterfeit," the most brilliant forger in Europe, a man whose genius for deception was matched only by his utter lack of scruple. A man who had been a rival, an occasional, untrustworthy collaborator, and ultimately, an enemy. A man who had disappeared from circulation two years ago, rumoured to be in prison, or dead.

And Popinot... Popinot had been Dubroc's right-hand man, his brutish enforcer, the iron fist to Dubroc's velvet glove.

The pieces clicked into place with sickening speed. The uninvited guests, Popinot's fanatical pursuit, her inexplicable fear and her talk of deception... it was not Lanyard they were primarily after. It was her. Or rather, it was something she possessed.

"Popinot is not hunting me," he stated, the words tasting like ash in his mouth. "He is hunting you."

She nodded, her face a pale mask of misery. "My father... before he disappeared... he trusted me with something. The culmination of his life's work. Plates, papers... the means to create a flawless series of British treasury notes. He told me to keep them safe, to use them only as a last resort. Popinot knows I have them. He believes my father is dead, and he wants them for himself. He has been hounding me for months."

"And you came to me," Lanyard said slowly, the enormity of the revelation crashing down upon him. "To the Lone Wolf. Not for protection, not really. You wanted to hire me. You wanted me to dispose of Popinot for you."

"No!" she cried, and for the first time, her composure broke. "No, not like that. At first, yes... I was desperate. I had heard the stories of you, of your final feud with your own syndicate. I thought you were a man who could... solve such problems. I sought you out. But then... I met you. I saw you that night at the opera, and I saw something else in your eyes. Not just a criminal, but a man who was weary of his own life. And when you spoke to me... everything changed. I saw a chance... not for me, but for you."

"A chance?" he echoed bitterly. "A chance to build my new life on a foundation of lies?"

"A chance to prove that you were right!" she insisted, her hands now gripping his coat, her knuckles white. "That you had something inherently decent in you! I knew Popinot would come. I knew there would be a confrontation. I thought, if you could face that, and not revert to... to the wolf... if you could find another way, a better way, for my sake... then your resolution would be real. It would be tempered in fire. It wouldn't be just an idea born in a moment of passion. It would be a fact."

He stared at her, dumbfounded. The sheer, mad logic of it was breathtaking. She had not merely deceived him; she had constructed an elaborate test, a moral crucible, using her own life, and his, as the raw materials. His quest for redemption, which he had thought so uniquely his own, had been a performance all along, staged and directed by her.

"And if I had failed?" he asked, his voice dangerously quiet. "If I had simply killed Popinot, as the Lone Wolf would have done?"

Her face crumpled. "Then I would have known... and I would have given him what he wanted, and disappeared. And you would have been free of me. And free of a lie."

"My God," he whispered, stepping back from her, from the wreckage of his newfound world. He looked from her tear-streaked face to the dark, flowing river, and then up at the indifferent moon. He felt as if there were nothing but emptiness beneath his feet. The sensation he had described to her in jest, in a warm and comfortable room that now seemed a part of some other man's life.

She had asked him if he would backslide. *How can I tell?* he had answered. He knew now. The old instincts were stirring, the cold, predatory logic of the Lone Wolf rising from its shallow grave. He could walk away. He could leave her to her fate with Popinot, take what little money he had left, and disappear back into the shadows that had been his only home. It was the sensible thing to do; the professional thing to do. She was not his love, his inspiration; she was a client, and a dangerously duplicitous one at that.

He looked at her again. She was no longer the serene icon of virtue he had worshipped, but a desperate, foolish, manipulative woman, caught in a trap of her own father's making. She was a lie.

And yet... and yet. Bourke's words came back to him: *The man who lets love into his life opens a door no mortal hand can close.* The door was open. He could not pretend it wasn't. And what had followed in was not the plaster saint of his imagination, but this, this infuriating, impossible, terrified woman.

He had told her it would take something damnable to shake his faith. This was surely that. He had told her that if he failed, it would be because he was unfit. The choice was before him. To leave her was to admit that his resolution was a sham, a thing so fragile it could be shattered by a single, disillusioning truth. To stay... to stay was madness. It was to embrace the very lie he had sworn to escape, to plunge back into the world of crime and deception, all for a woman who had used him from the start.

He thought of her in the restaurant, tracing patterns on the cloth. He thought of her in the doorway, a small, frightened shape in the dark. He thought of her hand-in-hand with him, two frightened children in a tunnel. The images were true, even if the names had been false. The fear was real. The danger was real.

"So," he said at last, his voice a low, rough thing he barely recognized as his own. "The Count of Counterfeit's daughter. And Popinot wants the plates." He gave a short, mirthless laugh. "It seems my retirement is to be... postponed."

She stared at him, her eyes wide with a dawning, incredulous hope. "You... you are not leaving me?"

He stepped forward and took her by the arms, his grip firm, proprietary. "Leave you?" he said, and there was a new, hard edge to his voice, the steel of a purpose reforged in the fires of disillusionment. "Lucia... I have just declared my intentions to you. A man cannot build a true life upon a foundation he has stolen; but perhaps, with a little work, he can make it his own."

The hand she had snatched away now rested upon the crumpled tablecloth, her fingers tracing the crease of a fold as if it were a line in a book of fates she could not decipher. Her gaze, when at last she raised it to his, was clouded with a sorrow so profound it eclipsed the candlelight.

"And what if," she began, her voice a near-whisper, "what if the very ground upon which you hope to build is not yours to claim? What if the inspiration, as you call it, is itself... a kind of theft?"

"I don't understand you," he said, and the bewilderment in his tone was genuine. The triumphant certainty that had buoyed him all evening was beginning to founder on the rocks of her strange, persistent melancholy. "Eleonora... what are you trying to tell me?"

"Perhaps only that you see me as a symbol," she continued, her eyes straying from his to some point in the middle distance, "a statue of virtue you have erected in your own mind. You are in love not with me, but with your own noble resolution; and I am merely the pedestal for it. And pedestals, Marcel... they are often made of very common stone."

The use of his old name, the name of the drudge, the shadow-dweller, struck him like a physical blow. He recoiled slightly, a frown knitting his brows. "That is not true. And it is not fair. I see you, the woman before me. The rest is... sophistry. You are trying to drive me away."

"Am I?" A wan smile touched her lips, a fleeting ghost of an expression. "Or am I trying to save you from a future disappointment so bitter it would poison the very memory of this night?"

Before he could formulate a reply, a rap on the door heralded the return of their waiter, a stout, cheerful man with a napkin draped over his arm. He entered bearing the bill on a small pewter plate, which he set down with a discreet cough and a murmured, "Whenever you are ready, Monsieur."

The intrusion, mundane as it was, shattered the tense intimacy of their exchange. It brought Lanyard crashing back to earth; to the reality of their situation, of the empty pocketbook and the watching city. He drew out his "emaciated purse" and counted out the notes, adding a tip that was, by his old standards, pitiably small, but which represented a significant portion of his remaining capital. The waiter, oblivious, beamed his thanks and departed.

There remained, as Lanyard had calculated, barely enough for a cab fare to some distant, hypothetical safety. The knowledge, which an hour ago had been a point of pride, a proof of his devil-may-care reliance on his own wits, now felt like a leaden weight in his stomach. His grand resolution seemed suddenly a flimsy, foolish thing in the face of her doubt and their shared penury.

"We should go," he said, his voice flat.

He helped her with her coat, his fingers brushing her shoulders. It was a gesture he had performed with a light heart only hours earlier; now it felt freighted with an unnameable significance, as if he were clothing a stranger. They descended the narrow, creaking stairs and passed through the now-empty dining room, its proprietor bidding them a sleepy "Bonne nuit."

Then they were outside, plunged once more into the damp embrace of the Parisian night. The mist had thickened into a fine, persistent drizzle that clung to their clothes and beaded in her hair. The lively clatter of Les Halles was a muted rumble in the distance; here, in the labyrinth of narrow streets, a profound silence reigned, broken only by the drip of water from a gargoyle's stone mouth and the soft echo of their own footsteps on the glistening cobblestones.

They walked without speaking, the chasm of their recent conversation yawning between them. Lanyard, his mind a turmoil of hurt pride and a dawning, terrible anxiety, steered them eastward through a warren of black alleys and sleeping courtyards he knew from another life; a life he had, only this evening, so confidently declared finished. The irony was not lost on him. He was using the knowledge of the Lone Wolf to guide the reformed man, a paradox that mirrored the very one she had thrown in his face.

"Where are we going?" she asked at last, her voice small in the vast quiet.

"Away from the main boulevards," he answered, not looking at her. "We cannot afford another cab, and the subways will be closing soon. We must walk. I thought... toward the river. We can follow it for a time; there is always cover there."

He felt the light pressure of her hand on his arm. "Marcel... I did not mean to..."

"Don't," he cut in, more harshly than he intended. He softened his tone. "Please. Let us not speak of it now. We are still not safe. Popinot's resources are not inconsiderable; it would be like him to have men watching the restaurants, even the small ones."

As if his words had conjured the threat, he saw it: a flicker of movement in the deep shadow of a porte-cochère fifty yards ahead. It was nothing, perhaps; a cat, a scrap of paper caught in the wind. But Lanyard's senses, honed by years of living on the knife-edge of peril, screamed a silent alarm. He halted so abruptly that she stumbled against him.

"What is it?" she whispered, her fear a palpable thing.

He did not answer immediately. His eyes, preternaturally sharp in the gloom, strained to dissect the shadows. He saw the man now, a silhouette, indistinct but for the tell-tale posture of one who waits. The man lit a cigarette, the brief flare of the match illuminating a narrow, rat-like face Lanyard knew all too well: a petty apache named Le Corbeau, a man who would sell his own mother for the price of a drink and who, Lanyard knew for a fact, had lately fallen into Popinot's orbit.

"A friend of our host," Lanyard murmured, his voice grim. He pushed her gently but firmly backward, into the deeper darkness of a recessed doorway. "Stay here. Do not move, and do not make a sound, no matter what happens."

His mind raced, sifting through possibilities with the cold, swift precision of a calculating machine. To fight was folly; Le Corbeau would not be alone. To run was to invite a chase they could not win on foot. There remained only guile; the old, familiar weapon he had sworn to lay down. Her words echoed in his head: *you've only to take one step aside to gain a smooth and easy way.* Was this it, then? The first test?

He glanced at her, a pale shape huddled in the doorway, her eyes wide and dark with terror. And in that moment, all the intellectual debate, all the philosophical wrangling of the past hour, evaporated. The question was no longer abstract. Her safety was the only axiom, the one fixed point in his reeling universe.

"I will be back," he whispered, and turning, he melted into the shadows, moving with a silent, fluid grace that was the antithesis of the honest, straightforward man he had resolved to become.

He did not go far. He circled the block, using an alley he remembered that ran behind the buildings. It was foul-smelling and slick with refuse, but it brought him out on a parallel street. From there, it was a simple matter to approach the porte-cochère from the opposite direction. He flattened himself against a wall, his heart pounding a slow, steady rhythm, his entire being focused on the task at hand. He was the Lone Wolf again, and he felt the grim, intoxicating thrill of the hunt.

He waited. Minutes stretched into an eternity. At last, he heard what he had been listening for: a low whistle from down the street, a signal. Le Corbeau straightened, flicked his cigarette into the gutter, and began to walk away from his post, heading toward the source of the sound. Lanyard gave him a twenty-second lead, then followed.

He shadowed the man for two blocks, to the corner of the rue de Rivoli. Here, another figure detached itself from the gloom of the arcades. The two men met, spoke in low tones. Lanyard was too far away to hear the words, but the gestures were plain enough: a shrug from Le Corbeau, an impatient chop of the hand from the newcomer. A report was being made; a failure was being admitted. Popinot's net had, for the moment, come up empty.

Lanyard watched them separate, Le Corbeau shuffling off into the night, the other man striding purposefully toward the Tuileries. Only then did he allow himself to breathe. He had gambled on Popinot's patience, and won. The search in this sector was being called off, at least for now.

He made his way back to the doorway where he had left her. The journey, which had taken him nearly fifteen minutes, seemed to have lasted a lifetime. He found her just as he had left her, a statue of terrified obedience pressed into the stone recess.

"It's all right," he said softly, his voice emerging as a croak. He cleared his throat. "They've gone. We are safe, for a little while."

She did not fly into his arms with relief. She simply sagged against the wall, a puppet whose strings had been cut. He reached out and took her arm, and this time she did not resist. Her flesh was cold as ice, even through the fabric of her coat.

"You were gone so long," she said, her voice trembling. "I thought..."

"I had to be certain," he said. "They were calling in the watchdogs. We have a few hours, perhaps, before they cast the net again. We must use them."

He led her out of the doorway and into the street. The drizzle had stopped, and a sliver of moon now shone through a ragged tear in the clouds, bathing the wet rooftops in a ghostly silver light. They walked on, their footsteps a lonely counterpoint to the city's sleeping heartbeat. The brief, sharp thrill of the chase had faded, leaving Lanyard with a sour taste in his mouth. He had not failed the test, perhaps; but he had not passed it in the way he had hoped. He had used the wolf's cunning to save the man, and he did not know whether to feel pride or shame.

They reached the Pont Neuf and paused, leaning against the cold stone parapet. Below them, the Seine flowed black and silent, its surface littered with shimmering reflections. In the distance, the skeletal form of the Eiffel Tower was a charcoal sketch against the clearing sky. Paris lay spread before them, a city of infinite beauty and infinite menace.

"Marcel," she said, her voice now steady, imbued with a strange, quiet resolution. "There is something I must tell you. Something you should have known from the beginning."

He turned to face her. Her profile was outlined against the moonlit water, as delicate and as remote as a cameo. "I am listening," he said.

"My name," she began, and her hesitation was so slight he almost missed it, "is not Eleonora Shannon."

Lanyard said nothing. He felt a peculiar stillness descend upon him, a profound and terrible calm. It was as if he had been anticipating this blow without knowing it; as if his body had been braced for it all along.

"My family is not... good. It is not even my family. The story I told you, of a young woman obliged to become self-supporting... it is a lie. Every word of it." She took a breath, a ragged, painful sound. "My real name is Lucia. And my father... my father is a man you know. Or a man you knew of, in your former life. His name is Count Victor Dubroc."

Lanyard felt the world tilt on its axis. Dubroc. The name echoed down the dark corridors of his memory. Victor Dubroc, the "Count of Counterfeit," the most brilliant forger in Europe, a man whose genius for deception was matched only by his utter lack of scruple. A man who had been a rival, an occasional, untrustworthy collaborator, and ultimately, an enemy. A man who had disappeared from circulation two years ago, rumoured to be in prison, or dead.

And Popinot... Popinot had been Dubroc's right-hand man, his brutish enforcer, the iron fist to Dubroc's velvet glove.

The pieces clicked into place with sickening speed. The uninvited guests, Popinot's fanatical pursuit, her inexplicable fear and her talk of deception... it was not Lanyard they were primarily after. It was her. Or rather, it was something she possessed.

"Popinot is not hunting me," he stated, the words tasting like ash in his mouth. "He is hunting you."

She nodded, her face a pale mask of misery. "My father... before he disappeared... he trusted me with something. The culmination of his life's work. Plates, papers... the means to create a flawless series of British treasury notes. He told me to keep them safe, to use them only as a last resort. Popinot knows I have them. He believes my father is dead, and he wants them for himself. He has been hounding me for months."

"And you came to me," Lanyard said slowly, the enormity of the revelation crashing down upon him. "To the Lone Wolf. Not for protection, not really. You wanted to hire me. You wanted me to dispose of Popinot for you."

"No!" she cried, and for the first time, her composure broke. "No, not like that. At first, yes... I was desperate. I had heard the stories of you, of your final feud with your own syndicate. I thought you were a man who could... solve such problems. I sought you out. But then... I met you. I saw you that night at the opera, and I saw something else in your eyes. Not just a criminal, but a man who was weary of his own life. And when you spoke to me... everything changed. I saw a chance... not for me, but for you."

"A chance?" he echoed bitterly. "A chance to build my new life on a foundation of lies?"

"A chance to prove that you were right!" she insisted, her hands now gripping his coat, her knuckles white. "That you had something inherently decent in you! I knew Popinot would come. I knew there would be a confrontation. I thought, if you could face that, and not revert to... to the wolf... if you could find another way, a better way, for my sake... then your resolution would be real. It would be tempered in fire. It wouldn't be just an idea born in a moment of passion. It would be a fact."

He stared at her, dumbfounded. The sheer, mad logic of it was breathtaking. She had not merely deceived him; she had constructed an elaborate test, a moral crucible, using her own life, and his, as the raw materials. His quest for redemption, which he had thought so uniquely his own, had been a performance all along, staged and directed by her.

"And if I had failed?" he asked, his voice dangerously quiet. "If I had simply killed Popinot, as the Lone Wolf would have done?"

Her face crumpled. "Then I would have known... and I would have given him what he wanted, and disappeared. And you would have been free of me. And free of a lie."

"My God," he whispered, stepping back from her, from the wreckage of his newfound world. He looked from her tear-streaked face to the dark, flowing river, and then up at the indifferent moon. He felt as if there were nothing but emptiness beneath his feet. The sensation he had described to her in jest, in a warm and comfortable room that now seemed a part of some other man's life.

She had asked him if he would backslide. *How can I tell?* he had answered. He knew now. The old instincts were stirring, the cold, predatory logic of the Lone Wolf rising from its shallow grave. He could walk away. He could leave her to her fate with Popinot, take what little money he had left, and disappear back into the shadows that had been his only home. It was the sensible thing to do; the professional thing to do. She was not his love, his inspiration; she was a client, and a dangerously duplicitous one at that.

He looked at her again. She was no longer the serene icon of virtue he had worshipped, but a desperate, foolish, manipulative woman, caught in a trap of her own father's making. She was a lie.

And yet... and yet. Bourke's words came back to him: *The man who lets love into his life opens a door no mortal hand can close.* The door was open. He could not pretend it wasn't. And what had followed in was not the plaster saint of his imagination, but this, this infuriating, impossible, terrified woman.

He had told her it would take something damnable to shake his faith. This was surely that. He had told her that if he failed, it would be because he was unfit. The choice was before him. To leave her was to admit that his resolution was a sham, a thing so fragile it could be shattered by a single, disillusioning truth. To stay... to stay was madness. It was to embrace the very lie he had sworn to escape, to plunge back into the world of crime and deception, all for a woman who had used him from the start.

He thought of her in the restaurant, tracing patterns on the cloth. He thought of her in the doorway, a small, frightened shape in the dark. He thought of her hand-in-hand with him, two frightened children in a tunnel. The images were true, even if the names had been false. The fear was real. The danger was real.

"So," he said at last, his voice a low, rough thing he barely recognized as his own. "The Count of Counterfeit's daughter. And Popinot wants the plates." He gave a short, mirthless laugh. "It seems my retirement is to be... postponed."

She stared at him, her eyes wide with a dawning, incredulous hope. "You... you are not leaving me?"

He stepped forward and took her by the arms, his grip firm, proprietary. "Leave you?" he said, and there was a new, hard edge to his voice, the steel of a purpose reforged in the fires of disillusionment. "Lucia... I have just declared my intentions to you. A man cannot build a true life upon a foundation he has stolen; but perhaps, with a little work, he can make it his own."
